notes.back:
No. `draw({ x: 1, y: 2, color: "red" })` fails: 'color' does not exist in type 'Point'. Passing the variable p compiles.

Why: An object literal written straight into a call gets an excess property check, since an unknown property there is probably a typo. A variable is just checked for having x and y.

Docs: TypeScript Handbook — Object Types — https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/objects.html
notes.quote: Object literals get special treatment and undergo excess property checking when assigning them to other variables, or passing them as arguments.

notes.back:
No. `const thing: Named = { title: "Rex" }` fails ('title' does not exist in type 'Named'). The Dog line compiles.

Why: TypeScript compares shapes, not class names: a Dog has a string name, so it is a Named. The literal has no name (and an unknown title).

Docs: TypeScript for JavaScript Programmers — https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/typescript-in-5-minutes.html
notes.quote: One of TypeScript's core principles is that type checking focuses on the shape that values have. This is sometimes called "duck typing" or "structural typing".
